rv.q: That nonstop naughtiness is what makes Martin McDonagh’s killer satire the best new play on Broadway by a green mile.

It’s a fabulous offering — a throwback, really, to the heyday of juicy, creepy London imports by McDonagh (“Pillowman”), Conor McPherson (“Shining City”), Mark Ravenhill and Jen Butterworth (“Jerusalem”).
Happily (if such a word would apply to any of his work), this Broadway production is a deadly beauty, flawlessly cast and directed in the mordant style of an executioner’s song by Matthew Dunster.
Mr. McDonagh is incapable of writing a dull character or a flaccid line of dialogue.
McDonagh’s cynicism feels closer to our own, or rather we to it.
Allen as Mooney hasn’t got the gravity, or the menace.
Beneath its slick coating, it's a slack exercise that in retrospect makes almost no sense at all.
“Hangmen” thoroughly wrings its premise dry, but anyone trying to find deeper meaning in McDonagh’s play will be left hanging.
“Hangmen” is this Broadway season’s best play.
Hangmen would make an excellent companion piece to Tracy Letts' The Minutes – at least for anyone looking to satisfy a hankering for the delightfully macabre.

“Hangmen” is a meticulously-plotted work containing eccentric characters and built upon elements of pub drama, physical farce, whodunit mystery, action thriller and legal drama – not to mention a noose and countless pints of cask ale.
But it’s a welcome callback to the plays that built contemporary theatre: sturdy, well-observed, and vividly performed.
Hilarious, searing, and poignant, the play presents a savage indictment of capital punishment without ever stooping to preach — a practice foreign to Mr. McDonagh.
But there's real pathos in between the lines and endless pints of lager — even maybe a little heart.
Nonetheless, Hangman remains a wickedly perverse delight for theatergoers possessing the stomach and fortitude to go along for the ride.
Broadway hasn't had a good thriller in a long while, and Hangmen fits that bill quite nicely.
Something is amiss overall. Hangmen does not work the way it did at the Atlantic Theatre Company.
But things have happened in the world since then, and I had a rush of reactions, none of which came close to amusement, when a character in “Hangmen” is being choked, and says “Can’t breathe.”
Luckily (if not unexpectedly), there’s a huge payoff in Act II, which is where McDonagh’s gifts for melding black comedy, tragedy and surprise come together with peerless skill.
There are only 90 minutes in The Minutes, but they are probably among the funniest and most thought-provoking on Broadway.
I don’t feel that Hangmen is his best play, but every one of them is absolutely worth the price of admission.
Macabre as this latter may sound, there’s no question Hangmen is a well-executed piece of capital entertainment.
While Hangmen originally played like a thriller Off Broadway, it is now that rare item, a comedy of menace that is extremely funny.
Martin McDonagh has been specializing in his own brand of bloodstained comedy for a quarter of a century now, so it's probably inevitable that the blood might get a little tired.

With its tired jokes and dated humor, Hangmen provides an easy laugh, but it’s a difficult watch for those of us trying to be better audiences; questioning and interrogating works of culture that don’t quite sit right with our conversations around contemporary politics.
